results.title: Is Usability Testing Qualitative Or Quantitative?-2025 Guide
results.content: This guide explains how to choose, how many users you need, what metrics to report (completion, time, SUS/SEQ), how to interpret heatmaps and scores, and when companies should run benchmarks versus discovery tests. If you’re new-ish to UX-or prepping for interviews-you’ve probably felt this: you run a test in a UX research platform, and suddenly a dashboard showers you with **percentages**, **misclick counts**, **time-on-task**, and a big composite **“usability score.”** Your gut says, “Ah, so usability testing is **quantitative**.” Then a senior researcher looks at your plan and says, “Nope-usability testing is **qualitative**; five users is enough.” It’s confusing, and the internet doesn’t help much because you can find smart people arguing both sides. Use quant to measure and compare performance (larger samples; predefined success rules; report completion/time with confidence intervals or against benchmarks). Here’s the reality you can say out loud in interviews and in stakeholder rooms without sweating: **usability testing can be qualitative** ***or*** **quantitative.** It depends on your **goal**, **study design**, and **sample size**-not on whether your tool shows numbers. When people say “**qualitative usability testing**,” they mean small, purposefully varied samples with rich observation (clips/quotes), aiming to **find and understand issues**. When they say “**quantitative usability testing**,” they mean larger samples with **predefined success rules** and **confidence intervals** around metrics like completion rate and time, often compared against a prior release or a competitor. They only become **inferential** (e.g., “we’re 90% confident real-world users will complete Task 3 at ≥80%”) when your **study was designed** for estimation or comparison and your **sample is large enough** to compute **confidence intervals** sensibly. Predefined success rules; reporting completion/time with 90% confidence intervals; SUS compared to prior benchmark.”**. * **Label:** “**Qualitative usability test (n=8, moderated).** Numbers are descriptive; findings are issue-focused and traceable to clips.”. * **Label:** “**Quantitative usability evaluation (n=30)** with predefined rules; reporting intervals and benchmarks.”. Usability testing is the practice of assessing the functionality and performance of your website, app, or product by observing real users completing tasks on. Use u003cstrongu003equantitativeu003c/strongu003e testing to measure and compare performance (larger samples; predefined success rules; report completion/time with confidence intervals or against benchmarks).

results.title: A Guide to Sample Sizes in UX Research — It’s Not “Test with 5”! | by Nate Cook | Bootcamp | Medium
results.content: # A Guide to Sample Sizes in UX Research — It’s Not “Test with 5”! Researchers should understand the fundamental principles that are the foundations of any guidelines or general rules, and when the general guidelines apply and don’t — To truly understand proper sample sizes, you need a foundational understanding of statistics (probability, inferential statistics, variability, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, confidence, power, effect sizes, etc.) Researchers ought to develop this knowledge if they have not. And since inferences from research is often desired and needed by product teams (we usually want to estimate the experience of the entire user population from a sample), sample size is a topic UX researchers should fully understand and carefully consider whenever planning research. Throughout my career, research sample size has been challenged by product leaders — more times than I can count. Research is almost always inferential in nature instead of merely descriptive — we don’t typically care to merely describe the small group (sample) of people we tested with — we want to generalize the findings to the user population. The moment you ask users to rate something on a scale, or use standardized surveys, like SUS, or count the number of participants who were successful in a task or encountered a specific usability problem, your research has now become quantitative (numerical) in nature, and thus, typically, increase sample sizes are required. * Test with 5, 3 times was for research with the intended objective of “**issue discovery**” — discovering and understanding usability issues — **NOT** for the collection of quantitative (numeric) data, like task success rates, error rates, user ratings on scales (e.g., SUS, SEQ, ASQ, UMUX, and others), issue fequency, etc. Unfortunately, a lot of quantitative metrics in usability research are often binary (such as task success rates or error rates), and this too typiucally requires a larger sample size for the same level of accuracy compared to continuous data. Because of the often mixed nature of usability research (wanting qualitative AND quantitative data — not just qualitative like Nielsen was talking about with “test with 5”), and because of the fast-paced world of Agile development (in which we don’t always have time to do 3 iterative tests), **sample sizes for usability tests should be about 15 people**.

results.title: Task Times in Formative Usability Tests – MeasuringU
results.content: # Task Times in Formative Usability Tests. It is common to think of time-on-task data gathered only during summative evaluations because, during a formative evaluation, the focus is on finding and fixing problems, or at least finding the problems and delivering a report. In this article, I show that time-on-task can be a valuable diagnostic and comparative tool during formative evaluations. 2. Average task-times are an inaccurate metric when users think-out-loud. 3. Task times are only for benchmarking and not for identifying problems. One *can* collect time-on-task and use parametric statistics for the small (<10) sample sizes in usability tests. For example, when calculating confidence intervals for task time, use t-statistics instead of the normal deviate (z-statistic) because t-statistics take into account the size of the sample in generating the interval. **In short, your sample size alone does not preclude the use of taking time-on-task metrics or using statistics to describe them.**. ### Task-Time as a Benchmark between Designs. If you are doing a formative evaluation as part of an iterative testing plan and you have used think-aloud during all iterations, the mean time-on-task becomes a benchmark to help judge the efficacy of subsequent designs. That is, assuming you use the same tasks and have users think-aloud concurrently with their task attempts, you can compare the mean completion times across iterations. Getting an accurate and stable measure of the actual user time-on-task is more problematic that comparing designs. One would expect task times to increase as users are asked to think-aloud while completing tasks. For example, the following task data graphed in Figure 1 were taken from the publicly available CUE-4 (Molich 2004) data from Team M, which timed 15 users while they thought-out-loud as they completed tasks on a hotel reservation website. One user took over 4 times the mean time to complete the task. In graphing the report we quickly see that one user took over 4 times longer than the mean time to cancel the reservation (I graphed the data using the Graph and Calculator for Confidence Intervals for Task Times). Time-on-task is an under-utilized tool for formative evaluations. I encourage you to collect time-on-task during your next formative evaluation.

results.title: A Practical Guide to Measuring Usability
results.content: There are generally two types of tests: finding and fixing usability problems (formative tests) and describing the usability of an application from average task times, completion rates and other metrics. As an example, see Task Times in Formative Usability tests: http://www.measuringusability.com/formative-time.php www.MeasuringUsability.com 10 Acknowledgements In a recent survey I sent to the subscribers of MeasuringUsability.com there was a 2 to 1 ratio between the frequency of formative and summative tests. The majority of usability testing involves having users attempt tasks and finding and fixing as many problems discovered during testing as time and funds allow (called formative evaluations). Instead you need to systematically record problems and use other metrics such as task times, completion rates, errors and satisfaction questionnaires to both diagnose and qualify usability problems.
